parts.note: read as a worker in gold stamping a mark on precious metal, not the writer Oliver Goldsmith making an impact

explanation.surface: Oliver Goldsmith, the writer, made a fine impression on his readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goldsmith' looks like the Irish author; read it as any smith working gold, and the 'impression' is the official stamp punched into gold or silver to certify its purity.
explanation.definitionFit: An assay office stamps this mark on precious metal articles, an impression a goldsmith's wares carry.

definitions.meaning: describes the crab that lives in a borrowed shell
Peter the ___ preached the First Crusade

explanation.surface: Peter walking sideways like a crab.
explanation.definitionFit: The crab living in a cast-off shell has this name, and Peter of Amiens was the Crusade preacher called it.

clue.text: The liberal muse ? Right for Simon Bolivar

parts.note: LIB is the abbreviation for Liberal
Erato is the Muse of lyric poetry

explanation.surface: A liberal-minded Muse is the right one for Simon Bolivar.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon Bolivar, who freed much of South America from Spanish rule, was called El Libertador.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolivar won independence for several South American nations and was hailed as their freer.

parts.note: refers to the fox terrier in Jerome K Jerome's 'Three Men in a Boat'

explanation.surface: A dog sitting in a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: In Jerome K Jerome's comic novel 'Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog)', the fox terrier is named this.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerome's 1889 comic novel of a Thames trip has a fox terrier as the fourth passenger.

parts.note: the head of 'red' is its first letter, R
Odin is the chief Norse god

explanation.surface: An artist who carved the god with red hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Redhead' reads as a ginger-haired person; split it as 'red head', the first letter of 'red'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French artist who made 'The Thinker' and 'The Kiss' in bronze and marble.

parts.note: in bridge, a player who makes no bid on their turn, spades or anything else, says the word for declining

explanation.surface: A bridge player let the chance to call spades slip by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Failed' points towards exams; in bridge the call made when you decline to bid is this word, the opposite of failing in the exam sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'no bid' at the bridge table is the call that lets the auction move on.

indicators.note: sounds signals that the word for good is heard, and the spelling of the dish is what goes in

parts.note: PI, short for pious, is crossword shorthand for good

explanation.walkthrough: 'Easy as ___' is a stock phrase, so the dish is the easy one; 'sounds good too' says it is heard as PI, crossword shorthand for pious.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastry-topped baked dish, proverbially simple in the phrase 'easy as ___'.

definitions.meaning: to dismiss an idea with contempt
a member of the youth movement whose members do a good turn daily

explanation.surface: Dismissing a well-meaning person with contempt.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismiss a proposal with contempt is one sense, and Baden-Powell's youth members pledge a daily good turn.

parts.note: Des is short for Desmond
cried, wept, means was unhappy

explanation.surface: Someone noticed that Desmond was upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Observed' looks like 'remarked'; it means caught sight of.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch sight of something in the distance is to spot or notice it.

parts.note: the nursery rhyme 'Who killed Cock ...?' answers 'I, said the Sparrow, with my bow and arrow'

explanation.surface: A small bird preys on another.
explanation.walkthrough: The old English nursery rhyme has the sparrow confess to shooting the red-breasted bird with a bow and arrow.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme the sparrow owns up to killing Cock ___, the red-breasted songbird.

parts.note: read as people who all sit 'a board', members of a company's governing board, not passengers boarding a train

explanation.surface: A guard's cry as the train is about to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: The railway call is the false path; split 'aboard' as 'a board' and it describes the members of a company board.
explanation.definitionFit: Company executives who sit together on the governing board are all 'on the board'.

clue.text: Explosive noises at the end of term

definitions.meaning: school accounts of a pupil's progress issued when term ends

explanation.surface: Bangs going off as the school term finishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunshots are loud bangs, and pupils take home written accounts of their progress when school breaks up.

parts.note: someone who pulls strings and controls others, and also literally a 'hand' man who works things with the hands

explanation.surface: A jobbing odd-job man with some clout.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for someone who exerts crafty influence comes from the Latin for 'handful', so it also fits a man who works with his hands, such as an osteopath.
explanation.definitionFit: A schemer controlling others exerts influence, and the word's root means working by hand.

parts.note: read as the March sisters Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy of Louisa May Alcott's novel, not girls who march

explanation.surface: Girls marching, perhaps in a parade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' looks like a verb or the month; it is the surname of the four sisters in Louisa May Alcott's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcott's 1868 novel follows the four March sisters growing up in New England.

parts.note: G K Chesterton's 'Song of Right and Wrong' says of the drink: 'although an Oriental, is a gentleman at least'

explanation.surface: A gentleman from the East appearing in a Chesterton story.
explanation.walkthrough: Chesterton's poem praises the Chinese drink over cocoa: it, 'although an Oriental, Is a gentleman at least.'
explanation.definitionFit: Chesterton's verse personifies the Chinese brew as an Eastern gentleman, unlike cocoa, a 'cad and coward'.

parts.note: a member of Britain's part-time Territorial Army has this nickname, which is also a breed of small hunting dog

explanation.surface: A dog used by the military.
explanation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army is Britain's volunteer reserve; its soldiers are nicknamed after the breed of dog, so 'Army dog' is both the soldier and the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A Territorial Army reservist shares a nickname with a small burrowing dog breed like the Jack Russell.

parts.note: a gap to fill from Rupert Brooke's poem 'Heaven', in which fish imagine their god

explanation.surface: Fill in the missing word of a line by Rupert Brooke.
explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Brooke's 'Heaven' imagines a fish deity: '___, of fishy form and mind, Squamous, omnipotent, and kind'.
explanation.definitionFit: Brooke's fish picture their god as vast in size, huge beyond measure.

clue.text: It's short and sweet in Battersea

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the place name Battersea, spanning its letters

explanation.surface: Something brief and pleasant found in Battersea, a district of south London.
explanation.walkthrough: Battersea is a district of south London; 'in' signals the answer lies within its letters, BatTERSEa.
explanation.definitionFit: Short and sweet describes speech that is brief and to the point, concise without waste.

clue.text: He's taking lambs to the slaughterhouse

definitions.text: He's taking lambs to the slaughterhouse

parts.note: taken as written, the letters H E S

explanation.surface: A butcher leads lambs off to the abattoir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To the slaughterhouse' rearranges HE'S and LAMBS; the whole clue also describes where the man is going, since the word once meant a meat market or slaughterhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The word once meant a meat market or abattoir, hence its modern sense of a bloody mess.

clue.text: Superman gets the point, and the bird

parts.note: Superman is the archetypal comic-book hero
N, north, is a compass point

explanation.surface: Superman understands the argument, and also the bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets the point' reads as understanding; here 'point' is a compass point, N, added to HERO.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-legged wading bird that stands in shallows spearing fish.

clue.text: Strength of a body of a hundred and fifty surrounded by nine

indicators.note: surrounded by means the 150 piece sits inside the nine piece

parts.note: there are nine Muses in Greek myth
CL is 150 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: The power of a group of 150 people hemmed in by nine others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body' suggests a group of people; the nine are the Muses, and CL (150) goes inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical power in a person's frame comes from its brawn, the tissues that contract.

definitions.meaning: a stock phrase or quotation, often Latin, tacked on to speech
the children's chasing game where 'it' touches others

explanation.surface: A game played with a Latin quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: A hackneyed Latin phrase is a stock saying, and the chasing playground game shares the word.

clue.text: A renegade among the American soldiery goes free

indicators.note: among places the turncoat inside the soldiers

a rat is a turncoat or deserter

explanation.surface: A deserter mingling with US troops gets away with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes free' reads as escaping; 'free' alone means without charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Something given at no cost is free of charge.

clue.text: That buffoon Aguecheek appears slightly tiddly

parts.note: merry means a little drunk
Sir Andrew Aguecheek is the foolish knight in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's foolish knight Aguecheek shows up a little drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tiddly' is British slang for tipsy; Sir Andrew Aguecheek is the comic knight of Twelfth Night, giving his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A clown or jester who entertains with antics, originally a quack's assistant at fairs.

parts.note: a man's name that is also the radio operator's word for 'message received'

explanation.surface: A radio operator acknowledges a signal.
explanation.walkthrough: In radio procedure the word means 'received', and it is also a man's name, hence 'He'.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio users say this to mean a transmission was received and understood.

clue.text: Campbell's rapid roller leaving its bed ?

definitions.text: Campbell's rapid roller leaving its bed ?

parts.words: Campbell's rapid roller leaving its bed
parts.note: Thomas Campbell's 'Hohenlinden' has 'Iser, rolling rapidly'; a river leaving its bed rises, and a person leaving bed gets up

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Campbell's poem 'Hohenlinden' speaks of the river 'Iser, rolling rapidly'; put R before ISER and you have someone getting out of bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone getting out of bed in the morning, early or late, gets up.

clue.text: Not the quality of heavy blows from the slings

indicators.note: blows means the letters of 'the slings' are scattered and rearranged, as by a blast

explanation.surface: Heavy blows from slings lack a certain quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blows' looks like the noun after 'heavy'; it is a verb, the anagram signal, rearranging THE SLINGS.

parts.note: Stephen Foster's song 'Camptown Races' has 'I bet my money on de bob-tail ...'

explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Foster's minstrel song 'Camptown Races' has the line 'Somebody bet on de bay' and 'I bet my money on de bob-tail ___'.
explanation.definitionFit: An old or poor horse; Foster's singer backs one with a docked tail.

indicators.note: into signals that the answer is found running inside the words 'some antique'

explanation.surface: Goods brought from abroad into some antique shops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imported' suggests foreign goods; here it means signified, and the answer lies inside soME ANTique.
explanation.definitionFit: To import is to signify or convey, so what was imported is what was intended.

clue.text: Racehorses can go and get knotted

definitions.text: Racehorses can go and get knotted

parts.words: Racehorses can go and get knotted
parts.note: a stable's racehorses are called by this word for a group, which is also cord that can be tied in knots

explanation.surface: A rude dismissal of some racehorses: get knotted!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get knotted' is a British rude dismissal; here it is literal, cord being tied, and a trainer's horses are collectively his ___.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainer's group of horses is his string, and twine or cord can be tied in knots.

parts.note: names Tennyson's long narrative poem about a royal lady who founds a women's college, its premise mocked as a fanciful idea

explanation.surface: A notion of Tennyson's that went nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's 1847 poem, subtitled 'A Medley', tells of a king's daughter who shuts herself away to found a university for women.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's poem takes its title from its heroine, a king's daughter, Ida.
